chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sama'ah, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I heard him (peace be upon him) saying: A man came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and said, 'O Messenger of Allah! I have performed Zihar with my wife.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Go, so emancipate a neck (slave).' He said, 'I have nothing.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Go, so fast for two consecutive months.' He said, 'I am not strong enough.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Go, so feed sixty poor ones.' He said, 'I have nothing (with me).' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'I shall give charity on your behalf,' and gave him dates for feeding sixty poor ones. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Go, so give in charity with it.' He said, 'By the One Who sent you with the truth, I do not know anyone between these two mountains more in need of it than myself and my family.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So go, eat and feed your family.'

key_terms.ظَاهَرْتُ: I performed Zihar (likening wife to mother)

ai.seo_question: What is the step-by-step expiation for Zihar in Shia jurisprudence when a person cannot afford the first option?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi elucidates the graduated scale of kaffarah for Zihar, highlighting the Prophet's pragmatic application of legal principles based on the individual's financial capacity. It underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the flexibility of expiation, where the obligation to feed the poor yields to the necessity of self-preservation when resources are critically scarce. The incident serves as a foundational precedent for understanding the interplay between ritual obligation and economic reality in Islamic jurisprudence.
